extracted.intended_audience: documentation specialists, librarians, information scientists, bibliographers, and publishers involved in indexing/scientometrics
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, compiling, and evaluating a citation index for the scientific literature (periodicals and optionally books), including coding schemes, coverage selection, mechanical processing, and the bibliographic/analytic uses of the index.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary purpose — reduce uncritical citation
rubrics_metrics.description: The citation index should eliminate the uncritical citation of fraudulent, incomplete, or obsolete data by making it possible for the conscientious scholar to be aware of criticisms of earlier papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the only use were minimizing citation of poor data, the index would be worth the effort. It helps locate bibliographic descendants and criticisms quickly so scholars need not spend inordinate time searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Association-of-ideas (bring together material beyond subject headings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The citation index is an association-of-ideas index that, by virtue of its different construction, tends to bring together material that would never be collated by the usual subject indexing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It gives readers more leeway than traditional subject headings and can surface cross-disciplinary links that classification or terminology-based indexing would miss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Granularity — index submicro (idea-level) units
rubrics_metrics.description: Whereas books and articles are macro and micro units of thought, a citation index deals in the submicro or molecular unit of thought—specific ideas or claims within articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This granularity is valuable because scientists are often concerned with particular ideas rather than whole concepts; conventional subject indexes cannot practically represent this level without overload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementary tool to subject and classified indexes
rubrics_metrics.description: A citation index is needed in addition to better alphabetical and classified indexes to help span the gap between document creators' subject approach and the scientist's information needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the citation index alongside conventional indexes; it is not a replacement but a complementary bibliographic tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part numerical coding for articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a simple numerical code to identify each scientific article: (1) a serial number for the periodical (replacing abbreviations), and (2) a serial article number within that periodical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This compact coding facilitates mechanical handling; drawbacks include no explicit year/volume and potential non-uniqueness of article numbers across journals—alternative coding schemes are possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core structure — periodical list + numeric citation listings
rubrics_metrics.description: Main characteristics: an alphabetic listing of all periodicals covered (with their code numbers) and a main portion listing in numerical order the code numbers for all articles; under each article code list code numbers of articles that have referred to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under each cited article, indicate whether the citing source is an original article, review, abstract, patent, translation, etc. This structure supports historical research and impact analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of citing source types
rubrics_metrics.description: Each citing reference should be annotated with the type of citing source (original article, review article, abstract, patent, translation, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enables filtering and interpretation of citations (e.g., whether influence is via reviews or original follow-up research).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation counts as impact/quantitative measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation listings provide a quantitative measure ('impact factor') of an article's influence and may be more indicative than raw publication counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use citation counts to evaluate relative importance of works; historical examples and existing journal-level measures are referenced for comparison and critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective coverage (define periodicals and period to include)
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage can be limited to a selected list of periodicals (e.g., those covered by established indexing services) rather than attempt exhaustive coverage of all 50,000+ titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selective coverage reduces workload and may even be advantageous by excluding less relevant peripheral titles; tradeoffs must be considered (e.g., Current List of Medical Literature, Chemical Abstracts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical volume planning and feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan for magnitude: millions of articles and citations per year are possible, but by limiting coverage to selected journals the annual number of citations to prepare becomes feasible (example: ~1 million citations/year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate expected citation volume from chosen coverage and ensure processing capacity (mechanical devices, staff) matches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher/author cooperation — unique article codes desirable
rubrics_metrics.description: If periodicals assigned unique article numbers and authors included them in bibliographies, indexing effort would be reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a long-term recommendation (unlikely under 5–10 years) comparable to advocating inclusion of Library of Congress card numbers by publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical processing and automation
rubrics_metrics.description: Handling large volumes requires high-speed mechanical devices (punched cards, sorting machines); mechanical approaches will likely determine success or failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While compilation can be done with conventional filing slips, mechanical methods substantially facilitate sorting and printing for large-scale indexes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Card-based coding procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Coding workflow: number every article in a journal, then for each citation prepare a 3x5 card containing (i) code of citing article, (ii) code of cited article, (iii) classification of the citing article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After coding, sort cards by cited-article code, then within each group by citing-article code; this yields complete citation listings ready for typesetting/printing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion rules — out-of-coverage items and books
rubrics_metrics.description: References to articles not in the prescribed list of journals should be excluded; books are excluded unless coverage specifies otherwise (in which case use LC card number as identifier).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly define coverage policy up front; if books are included, use Library of Congress card numbers as book codes to integrate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor and staffing model — unskilled coders plus professional oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: Relatively unskilled persons can do the mechanical coding and filing, but professional supervision is required for decisions needing skilled judgment (e.g., interpreting 'ibid.' or loc. cit., handling footnotes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the workforce and training so that routine tasks are delegated while experts handle ambiguous bibliographic interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value for historical and interdisciplinary research
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation indexing is particularly useful for historical research (measuring influence) and for discovering cross-disciplinary or peripheral references that subject indexes miss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include tracing how an idea is cited across disparate fields (RCA reading-aid example), and finding unexpected citations outside a paper's main subject area.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use-case — author 'clipping service' and awareness of who cites you
rubrics_metrics.description: An author can use citation listings to determine which other scientists refer to his/her work, improving communication and revealing implications previously unnoticed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide authors with their article's citation entry so they can track reception, reviews, and subsequent developments referencing their work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage over exhaustive subject indexing — leverages authors as indexers
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of attempting impossibly fine-grained subject indexing, a citation index uses authors' own references as a distributed indexing activity—each reference reflects an author's point of view and interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review articles are especially valuable since each bibliographic statement with its reference resembles indexed and critiqued entries; this reduces the need for paragraph-level indexers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sorting/printing preparation (post-coding steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: After coding and sorting the citation cards (by cited item then by citing item), the next step is preparation of the entries for the printer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the output format includes code numbers, full periodical list, and classification markers for citing sources; plan typesetting/printing workflow accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and realistic expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: A citation index is a valuable starting point in literature research but will not solve all bibliographic problems; do not expect it to be a universal solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the index as one tool among others (subject indexes, bibliographies, full reading) and communicate its strengths and boundaries to users.
